meta.title: Who really said "My conscience won't let me go shoot my brother, or some darker people, or some poor hungry people in the mud, for big powerful America"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Muhammad Ali, from a filmed interview apparently made just after his April 1967 induction refusal. But the "No Viet Cong" line usually attached to it is not his.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'My conscience won't let me go shoot my brother, or some darker people, or some poor hungry people in the mud, for big powerful America'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Ali, on film, apparently just after his April 1967 induction refusal. The famous "No Viet Cong ever called me..." line bolted onto it is probably apocryphal.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real, and it is on film. Slate’s Stefan Fatsis — who went looking specifically to separate Ali’s genuine Vietnam lines from the invented ones — transcribed this passage from an interview that, in his words, “appears to have been conducted shortly after Ali refused military induction in April 1967,” footage later used in a 1980 documentary by the WABC-TV series Like It Is. The popular text differs from that transcription only in punctuation.
answer.confidenceText: Ali said it, on camera. The exact date is the soft part — and the famous line usually bolted onto it is not his.

source.heading: The footage

docMeta.dd: Filmed interview, apparently soon after 28 April 1967
Like It Is (WABC-TV, New York), 1980 documentary
Genuine Ali — unlike the line often printed beside it

source.excerpt: My conscience won’t let me go shoot my brother, or some darker people, or some poor, hungry people in the mud, for big, powerful America, and shoot them. For what? They never called me n*****. They never lynched me. They never put no dogs on me. They never robbed me of my nationality, or raped and killed my mother and father. … How can I shoot them poor people? Just take me to jail.
trail: 17 February 1966, Miami. Ali gives the remark that starts the legend. Robert Lipsyte of the New York Times, writing later in a May 1967 Times Magazine profile, recorded that Ali was asked about the Vietcong, shrugged, and said “I got no quarrel with them Vietcong” — quoted by Stefan Fatsis ↗.

28 April 1967, Houston. Ali refuses three times to step forward for induction; he is convicted on 20 June 1967, and the Supreme Court reverses the conviction unanimously in Clay v. United States on 28 June 1971, per Wikipedia’s account ↗.

1967, on camera. Ali gives the interview containing this passage. Fatsis writes that it “appears to have been conducted shortly after Ali refused military induction in April 1967” and “was part of a 1980 documentary by the black public affairs television program Like It Is” — a WABC-TV New York series that ran from 1968 to 2011 ↗.
June 2016. After Ali’s death, Slate and later Professor Buzzkill ↗ separate the genuine material from the invented: this passage stands, the “No Viet Cong ever called me…” sentence does not.
source.excerptNote: As printed by Stefan Fatsis in Slate. The version that circulates online drops two commas — “poor hungry people” and “big powerful America” — and usually stops at “America.” The racial slur is rendered here as Professor Buzzkill renders it; the sources print it in full.

source.rightsNote: These are spoken words from a 1967 filmed interview whose surviving publication is a 1980 television documentary — both far later than the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff, so nothing here is public domain. Ali’s name, likeness and media library are managed through Muhammad Ali Enterprises, which Authentic Brands Group acquired in 2013 ↗ alongside “the largest library of photos and videos of the boxer”; the broadcast recording carries its own separate copyright. Quoted here for attribution research and commentary.

author.name: Muhammad Ali
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Muhammad Ali
author.metaLine: 1942–2016 · American heavyweight champion, Nation of Islam convert & conscientious objector
author.bio: Born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. in Louisville, Kentucky on 17 January 1942, Ali won the heavyweight title in 1964, joined the Nation of Islam and took his new name, and then spent the back half of the decade fighting the United States government instead of other boxers. On 28 April 1967 he refused three times to step forward for induction in Houston; he was convicted on 20 June 1967, stripped of his title, and barred from the ring for most of his physical prime. The Supreme Court reversed the conviction unanimously in Clay v. United States on 28 June 1971. He died on 3 June 2016.

misattribution.heading: What gets bolted onto it
misattribution.intro: The passage itself is sound. The trouble is what travels with it — a famous sentence Ali probably never said, a plainer sentence he definitely did, and a date that keeps changing depending on who is reposting.

items.scope: The line usually printed next to it
items.who: “No Viet Cong ever called me n*****”
items.why: Wikipedia flags this half of the famous formulation as “probably apocryphal,” and Stefan Fatsis found no evidence Ali coined it. Instead, Fatsis reports ↗ that on 23 February 1966, six days after Ali’s Miami comments, the Times covered a New York anti-war protest where one demonstrator carried a sign reading “The Viet Cong Never Called Me Nigger.” The originator is unclear; Stokely Carmichael is sometimes named.

items.scope: What Ali actually said in Miami
items.who: “I got no quarrel with them Vietcong”
items.why: Robert Lipsyte of the New York Times, who was there on 17 February 1966, later wrote that after hours of questioning Ali “admitted that he wasn’t sure where Vietnam was,” was asked about the Vietcong, shrugged, and said the line — a far plainer sentence than the one legend supplies, as Slate documents ↗.

Reposts variously date this passage to 1966 or to a specific March 1967 New York press conference. Neither is documented. The most careful account, echoed by Professor Buzzkill ↗, is simply that it comes from a 1967 interview — with Fatsis placing it after the April 1967 induction refusal and hedging even that.

misattribution.truthLine: Ali really did say the words in this quote, on camera. He almost certainly did not say the more famous sentence people attach to it — and the reporting that establishes both ↗ is the same piece of work.

context.heading: Why it cost him everything
lead: Ali was not making a speech when he said this. He was answering for a decision he had already made and was already paying for: on 28 April 1967 he had stood in a Houston induction centre and refused three times to step forward when his name was called. He was convicted on 20 June 1967 and lost his heavyweight title and his licence to fight.

What makes the passage land is that it is an argument, not a slogan. Ali is not saying war is wrong in the abstract — he is asking why a Black man from Louisville should be sent to kill poor people who had never done to him what America had. The Supreme Court reversed his conviction unanimously in Clay v. United States on 28 June 1971.
detailsBody: Like It Is was a public affairs television programme focusing on issues relevant to the African-American community, produced and aired on WABC-TV in New York City between 1968 and 2011 — one of the longest-running locally produced shows of its kind. It was co-hosted at first by the actor Robert Hooks and the WABC-TV reporter Gil Noble, with Noble becoming sole host and producer after 1975.

That archive is a large part of why this passage is checkable at all. A great many Ali quotations circulate only as text passed between quote sites; this one exists as a recording of the man saying the words, which is why it can be graded verified while the sentence usually printed beside it cannot.
